name: Scrotal cooling / ball icing

card.summary: Chilling the testes with ice or cold packs to support sperm or testosterone; rooted in real testicular physiology but untested as a practice.
card.aka: ball icing, testicle cooling, cold exposure for testes
card.note: No studies found; excessive cold can injure skin, and the body already regulates scrotal temperature.

quick.overview:
Scrotal cooling, or 'ball icing', is a fringe practice of applying cold to the testes in the hope of improving sperm quality or testosterone. It draws on the established fact that the testes work best a few degrees below core body temperature.

No studies were found testing deliberate cooling in healthy men for these goals. Its logic is an extension of heat-and-fertility research rather than evidence for the practice.
quick.mechanism: The scrotum normally keeps the testes around two to three degrees Celsius below core temperature, adjusting with the cremaster muscle and dartos fascia. Proponents reason that extra cooling will help sperm production. Reference sources say heat impairs spermatogenesis but do not say that further cooling improves it.
quick.risks: Reported or plausible concerns include skin cold injury from direct ice contact and the cremasteric reflex that draws the testes upward in cold. The body's own regulation already maintains testicular temperature, and the effect of extra cooling in healthy men has not been studied in the sources reviewed.

lead: Scrotal cooling, informally 'ball icing', is a fringe practice in which men apply ice, cold packs or cold water to the scrotum, hoping to improve sperm quality or testosterone. It is discussed in biohacking and fertility-optimisation circles and occasionally on looksmaxxing forums.

The idea builds on documented physiology: the scrotum keeps the testes about two to three degrees Celsius below core body temperature, and higher temperatures affect spermatogenesis.[1][2] The testes are moved toward or away from the body by the cremaster muscle, and the scrotum tightens in cold.[1][2]
No human studies of deliberate cooling in healthy men were found, so the practice's benefits are untested, though the underlying heat sensitivity of sperm production is well established.

paras: Practitioners describe brief applications of cold to the scrotal area. The rationale offered is that cooler testes mean better sperm production, extending the known effects of heat. Details vary by account, and sources suitable for citation were limited to general reference material.

The scrotum holds the testes at about 35 C, a few degrees below the core temperature of 37 C. The cremaster muscle and the dartos fascia adjust the testes' distance from the body, and the scrotum usually tightens in cold.[1]

Another reference says sperm production is most efficient slightly below core temperature, with efficiency falling both below and above about 33 C, and that temperatures above roughly 36.7 C impede it.[2] In mice, brief scrotal heat stress caused DNA damage, reduced fertility and abnormal embryonic development.[2] A fertility reference reports that sustained high ambient temperature consistently lowers sperm quality in animals and links heat to lower sperm quality in humans.[3]
Leydig cells in the testes produce testosterone under pituitary luteinizing hormone control.[2]
Related research concerns the effects of heat on spermatogenesis, in humans and animals, but not deliberate cooling of healthy men.[2][3]

The sources reviewed do not describe cooling-specific harms. General concerns include skin cold injury from direct ice contact. Reference sources also note that the cremasteric reflex raises the testes in response to cold.[2]

lore.intro: Cooling the testes appears in fertility and testosterone biohacking discussions as a counterpart to avoiding heat. No forum sources suitable for citation were available.

claims.claim: Cooling the testes improves sperm production.
claims.believers: Proponents reason that sperm thrive below body temperature, so more cooling should help.
claims.experts: References report that heat impairs spermatogenesis and that efficiency falls both below and above about 33 C; none describes benefit from additional cooling.[1][2]

claims.believers: Some advocates say cold supports testicular hormone output.
claims.experts: Leydig cell testosterone production is described as regulated by pituitary luteinizing hormone; no studies of cooling were found.[2]

claims.claim: Heat harms sperm, so cooling is protective.
claims.believers: Practitioners cite heat-related declines in semen quality.
claims.experts: Heat is associated with lower sperm quality in humans and animals, although the cited reference does not give study details.[3]
